div.p: Real-time applications are becoming more and more demanding in t e m of the computational power needed and the U0 bandwidth required. Massively parallel computers using wormhole routing are the most promising architectures to deliver scalable computational power efjiciently. It follows that real-time applications will want to take advantage of these architectures. Howevel; before real-time applications can exploit massively parallel architectures, mechanisms to ensure that critical hard deadline messages meet their deadlines need to be developed. An off-line feasibility test for real-time wormhole routed messages is presented. The test will work for any static priority assignment scheme. The effectiveness of several proposed priori0 assignment methods is evaluated using random (unqorm) traffic patterns. Simulations using a jlit level simulator (FLS) are pe~ormed to validate the test. Simulations show that a high degree of schedulability can be achieved with ajnite number of virtual channels, and that packetizing long messages increases the overall schedulability of the network.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In real-time applications, a computation's correctness depends not only on its results, but also on when the outputs are generated. Therefore real-time systems should have guarantees on when certain tasks complete. The notion of a deadline is used to measure the timeliness of task completion. The issue of real-time task scheduling has been studied in some detail. Rate monotonic scheduling [ 13 (RMS) has been shown to be a very successful uniprocessor real-time task scheduling algorithm. RMS assigns fixed priorities to tasks as a monotonic function of a tasks rate, with the most on bus based multiprocessor networks [2], as well as to simple ring connected distributed memory networks [3,4]. However, as real-time applications become more demanding, they will require the increased computational power and U 0 bandwidth offered by modern massively parallel computers.

Processors connected by a direct network (such as a mesh or cube) communicate by sending messages. Wormhole routing [SI is used as the flow control mechanism for second generation massively parallel computers, such as the Intel Paragon, and Cray T3D. Wormhole routing has improved latency characteristics compared to store-and-forward (S&F) routing. Wormhole routed messages are divided into small data units calledjlits [6] and pipelined through intermediate routers. Virtual channels (VCs) [6] are small data queues with associated state information that are used to store flits of a message at intermediate nodes. Figure 1 shows a 2dimensional mesh-connected wormhole routed network. A message is shown routing from the source node through routers at intermediate nodes to the destination node.

This research explores the applicability of wormhole routed architectures to real-time parallel computing, where tasks as well as messages need to meet their deadlines. A set of messages is determined to be feasible if, under assumed condlitions, all messages are guaranteed to be delivered by their deadline. Each message (Mi) is assumed to have a period (pi), a deadline ( d i ) , a maximum size (si), and a static priority that is the same for each instance of Mi. Messages are routed using deterministic routing.

Kandlur et a1 171 analyze interprocessor communication for real-time systems with a direct network using S&F routing. They present a method for guaranteeing maximum Figure 1. Wormhole routed message in a 3x3 mesh end-to-end delivery times for messages, and a schedulability test to ensure that real-time messages meet their deadlines. However, as mentioned earlier, wormhole routing has advantages over S&F routing.

Mutka et a1 [8,9, 101 present several flow control methods for real-time wormhole routed networks. Since most of these methods have no guarantees on the feasibility of messages, they are more suited to soft deadline systems than hard deadline systems. Mutka also presents one method for determining the feasibility of periodic wormhole routed messages that are assigned fixed priorities using the RMS algorithm, i.e., messages with shortest period have highest priority [8,9]. Priorities are assigned to messages based on the inverse of their period and the deadline of the message is equal to the period. The feasibility of each message is checked using the RMS test at each node of the message's path. div.head: A New Feasibility Test
div.p: Let Mi = (Ci, pi, di), i = 1, 2, ..., IC be the set of IC periodic messages, where Ci is the transmission time required for message Mi, with period p i , and deadline di .

For wormhole networks, C i can be approximated to silB, where si is the maximum size of Mi and B is the bandwidth of a physical link in the network. Let S i be the set of higher priority messages that share at least one link with Mi. For this research, it is assumed that there are as many virtual channels per link as messages per link and that links in the network are arbitrated based on priority. Therefore, a message cannot be blocked due to not being able to access a virtual channel. A message Mi can only be blocked, from accessing a link, by higher priority messages that share a link with Mi, (i.e., any message Mj E Si; j < i). Mi may be blocked by more than one instance of each Mj E Si since messages are periodic. The maximum end-to-end delivery time of Mi is the sum of the blocking time plus Ci. If this delivery time is less than the deadline, then the message is feasible, i.e., it is guaranteed to meet its deadline. The delivery time, Di(t), of Mi at time t is given as:

FTl is a sufficient condition for feasibility, but is not a necessary condition and can therefore be considered a pessimistic feasibility test. FTl considers the blocking at each link even if the blocking overlaps with the blocking that occurs at other links. A better test would consider this blocking only once. However, such a test would have to construct the worst-case phasing for each message, in order to arrive at a sufficient condition. Constructing such a phasing is a computationally difficult problem.

div.head: Priority Assignment
div.p: FT1 works for any static priority assignment method. However, it is desirable to find an optimal priority assignment strategy. RMS [l] assigns the highest priority to the task with the shortest period and has been shown to be an optimal static scheduling algorithm for scheduling real-time tasks on a uniprocessor [ 11. RMS can also be shown to be optimal for scheduling messages on a single link. However, RMS is not always an optimal priority assignment method for wormhole routed messages that traverse multiple links.

Heuristic priority assignment methods may produce better results than RMS in some cases. Mutka [ 101 proposed using the amount of blocking, a message can tolerate, or laxity of a message, to assign priority. Laxity is defined by li = di -Cj. Priorities could be assigned based on li, with the highest priority going to the messages with the smallest li. Heuristics could also take into account the number of hops a message travels. Thus, the priority of messages that travel a long distance would be increased since it is likely that they will encounter more blocking. Table 3 gives five possible heuristic functions for determining priority. Messages returning the lowest value for the heuristic function are given the highest priority.

H1 simply uses the laxity of a message to determine the priority. H2 and H3 use laxity and the number of hops that a message travels to determine priority. H4 and H5 use RMS and the number of hops to determine priority. H2, H3, H4 and H5 increase the priority of messages that traverse more hops.

However, as shown above, assigning priorities to messages based on RMS does not result in msg-c meeting its deadline under all circumstances. The RMS test is insufficient since it assumes that the highest priority task (or message in this case) that is ready to run can use a resource (physical link in this case). However, for wormhole routed networks the resource (physical link) may not be usable by the highest priority message ready to be sent, since that message may be blocked/suspended at some other link (as is the case in Example 1). An 8x8 mesh was used for all simulations presented. Network parameters are given in Table 4. Injection and consumption channels have the same bandwidth as physical links. A multiport model is assumed, and the number of injection and consumption channels per node is equal to the number of virtual channels used in each simulation. If messages are broken into packets, then a new header is created for each packet. Each packet needs to incur the setup cost of header processing times at each hop. However the time to break messages into packets at the source and reconstruct packets at the destination is ignored for the simulations run.

div.head: . Network Parameters
div.p: Random sourcddestination pairs were chosen for each message. Message size was chosen from 4 sizes (16, 128, 1024, or 4096 flits) with each size being equally likely. Depending on the message size, the period is chosen (from a set of 16 periods, 2mslooms), such that large messages are more likely to have long periods and short messages are more likely to have short periods. Original message lists are created by generating messages until a predefined average link bandwidth utilization (LBU) is achieved. The In general, using laxity and using RMS as priority assignment criteria performed about equally in terms of average LBU and number of messages that were schedulable using FTl. Taking into account the distance a message traveled when determining priority, resulted in higher LBU for the feasible message set, but fewer messages were included in the feasible set. This is because messages that travel several hops are given the highest priorities and scheduled first, resulting in more messages per link, but fewer overall messages. If the primary goal is to maximize the link utili:zation, then taking into account distance traveled is a good heuristic. If the primary goal is to maximize the number of feasible messages, then taking into account distance traveled is not a good heuristic. While no single heuristic number of original messages simulated performed better than the others for both link utilization and number of scheduled messages, all heuristics performed much better than random priority assignment for both link utilization and number of scheduled messages.

FTl assumed that there were as many VCs as messages per link. However, this is not a very realistic assumption. The messages that passed the feasibility test were therefore simulated using a finite number of virtual channels. Each message, Ma, has its first instance start at time zero and each subsequent instance of Ma started at the period of Ma. Simulation was run for 2 times the longest period so that each message would have at least two instances. Figures 7 and8 plot the ratio of messages that missed their deadline against the average LBU for different number of virtual channels available using the RMS and H3 priority assignment methods. As expected, the ratio of missed messages decreased as the number of available virtual channels increased. For the RMS method, an average LBU of 0.44, resulted in an average of 4 1.9 messages per link with the busiest link having 65 messages and the least used link having 20 messages. Thus, 65 VCs per link are required to guarantee message schedulability according to FTl, However, simulations showed that for this example, using 12 VCs resulted in no missed messages, and using 6 VCs resulted in about 1 in 500 message instances missing their deadlines. For the H3 priority assignment message list, using 12 VCs with a 0.45 average LBU resulted in about 1 in 10,000 message instances missing their deadline, and using 6 VCs resulted in 1 in 350 message instances missing there deadlines.

Simulations were only run for a finite amount of time, therefore they could not simulate the worst case blocking for each message. However, injecting all messages into the network at time zero should be a near worst case for each It is encouraging that using only 12 VCs was enough to result in no missed messages for all utilization levels and priority assignment methods simulated, except for the H3 priority assignment method at the highest utilization level.

Packetizing long messages (to a maximum size of 128 flit packets) reduced the ratio of missed messages greatly. For all demand levels and priority assignment methods, using only 4 VCs with packetized messages resulted in no missed messages. Although packetizing introduces additional overhead (due to increased setup times), it also helps to free virtual channels more often. It has been argued that the benefits of breaking messages into packets may not be worth the cost for non-real-time wormhole routed networks [ 121. For real-time wormhole routed messages, packetization provides natural preemption points in an otherwise non-preemptable network. Very large packets were used for the simulations (128 flits). Most current wormhole routed machines that break messages into packets use much smaller packets. Larger packets incur less overhead, however they provide fewer preemption points. Smaller packet sizes allow for more preemption points at the expense of greater overhead. The optimal size of a packet will depend on network as well as application factors, including header processing time and message generation characteristics.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: A feasibility test (FTl) for real-time wormhole routed messages was presented. FT1 works for any static priority assignment method. FT1 is a sufficient, but not necessary scheduling test. A goal for future research is to find a necessary condition, or at least relax the sufficiency condition. Assigning static priorities to messages based on period (RMS) is not always optimal for wormhole routed messages.
However, RMS performed about as well as the other priority assignment heuristics proposed. RMS and all heuristics performed much better than randomly assigning priorities to messages.

FT1 has a restrictive assumption that there are as many virtual channels per link as messages per link. It was shown through simulation, that if fewer VCs than messages per link are available, the messages still achieve a very high degree of schedulability (very low percentage of missed messages). However, for hard real-time systems, guarantees are needed for messages. Methods to bound the blocking that occurs when a finite number of VCs is used need to be developed. Feasibility tests that accurately calculate this worst-case bounded blocking need to be generated.

Packetizing messages greatly reduced the percentage of missed messages for all simulations run. This is because packet boundaries provide natural preemption points for higher priority messages to gain access to network resources (links).
